title: Five competitor dossiers for Arata
gives: Dated, sourced profiles of Traya, Pilgrim, Minimalist, Bare Anatomy and Mamaearth, built so every ad, comparison page and buyer pitch argues against what those brands actually say and charge today.
live: Five competitor profiles and a cross-competitor summary are live in a shared folder, a dated raw-data archive sits behind them, a monthly re-profile runs on a calendar, and the Arata vs Traya page, the MitoActive ads and the quick-commerce pitch all cite verified competitor prices and claims.

blocks.text: In SaaS this discipline means scraping rival pricing pages and pulling domain-authority data. For Arata it means profiling the five brands that sit next to it on a Blinkit search, a Nykaa listing, an Amazon.in "customers also viewed" row and a Meta feed: Traya, Pilgrim, Minimalist, Bare Anatomy and Mamaearth. The pages we read are product pages and hair-test funnels. The "reviews" are Nykaa and Amazon ratings. The method is the same. Facts first, inference labelled, implications framed as choices.

Today Arata's view of its competitors is a paragraph. The brand brief carries one line per rival: Pilgrim has "no clinical number", Minimalist is a "cold brand", Traya is "expensive, slow, medicalised". Those lines are probably right. None of them is dated, sourced or specific enough to put in an ad. The objection script for "₹1,499 for 30 ml is a lot" says to compare MitoActive to Traya at ₹1,400 to ₹1,800 a month. Traya's own cost page, read this week, puts the six-month plan at ₹1,400 a month, which is ₹47 a day. MitoActive at ₹1,499 for a 30-day bottle is ₹50 a day. The comparison Arata planned to make on price is a comparison it loses by ₹3. The comparison it wins is on commitment: one bottle versus a five-month lock-in with minoxidil, supplements and a refund that only pays out if you never miss a month. That is the kind of detail a dossier catches and a paragraph does not.

The cost of running without profiles shows up in three places. The planned "Arata vs Traya" and "Arata vs Pilgrim" pages will quote prices that drift within a quarter. The MitoActive launch, which already has zero reviews, will be argued against the wrong rival (Pilgrim's ₹699 serum) when the customer paying ₹1,499 is actually weighing Traya and minoxidil. And the quick-commerce category pitch, where 30% of revenue lives, needs a clean answer to "why you and not Mamaearth on the shelf" that is grounded in what Mamaearth's listing says today.

The opportunity is bigger than defence. Arata is the only brand in the ₹350 to ₹700 band that prints a study number on every bottle. Minimalist prints a percentage of actives. Pilgrim prints an ingredient list. Bare Anatomy prints a quiz result. Mamaearth prints "goodness". Traya prints a number, but behind a doctor, a kit and ₹8,400. The profiles below show that gap in a table, which is where it becomes a positioning decision rather than a belief.

What follows: five profiles built from the brief and three dated public lookups, a side-by-side comparison, a positioning map, the system that keeps the profiles current, and four finished assets Arata can use the week this lands.
How the profiles are built
Every profile keeps three layers apart, and the labels travel with the fact when it is reused in an ad or a page.

blocks.text: Two rules apply throughout. Not observed is not absent: if a competitor's page did not show a feature, the profile says "not observed on [pages checked], as of [date]" and the gap is confirmed before it goes into a public comparison. And we never state motive. We record that Minimalist sells at ₹699 and that Pilgrim lists a 12-ingredient story. We do not claim why.

Profile 1: Traya (traya.health)
**Depth:** deep profile. **Priority:** 1. This is the brand a ₹1,499 MitoActive buyer is actually weighing.

head: At a glance
Value
Source
rows: "Get the Best Hair loss Treatment & Diagnosis"

blocks.text: **Positioning.** Diagnosis first, then a customised kit. The funnel opens with a "FREE 2-minute hair test" that reads "20+ factors like genetics, scalp health, and lifestyle", asks for a scalp photo, and returns a plan in about five minutes. The product is the plan. The copy frames the purchase as "an investment in your hair's healthy future". Target audience signals: men and women with staged hair loss (the site uses Norwood-style stages 1 to 5), heavy tier-2/3 skew per the brief.
**Pricing (observed, traya.health cost page, 10 Oct 2026).**

The same page states a monthly range of ₹1,800 to ₹3,000, and a disclaimer shows starting prices of ₹1,699 and ₹2,000 per month for two sample 23 to 25-year-old male profiles. These three figures do not reconcile. We record the inconsistency rather than pick one. A worked example on the page prices a Stage 5 kit at ₹2,050 for six products: Minoxidil 2% (₹430), a nasal drop (₹150), a gut supplement (₹200), scalp oil (₹450), anti-dandruff shampoo (₹300) and an oral "hair ras" (₹520). Each kit is valid for 30 days.

**Guarantee and claims (observed).** "100% Money back guarantee if you see no results after five months of consistent use." Conditions: the full customised plan, five consecutive months, consistency checked against order dates, exclusions for autoimmune conditions and cancer. Results claims: "93% saw results" from an internal study dated December 2022; "3X better hair density" versus minoxidil 5% alone from a study of 1,200 men aged 21 to 40 at Stages 1 to 4. Stated treatment window: 5 to 9 months.

**Inferred (high confidence).** The pricing table is built to move customers to the 6-month plan. The guarantee is structured so the refund requires five paid months in sequence, which means the minimum spend to qualify is ₹7,000 to ₹9,000. The kit mixes a regulated active (minoxidil), ingestibles and topicals, which is why the brand needs doctors in the loop.

**Strengths.** Largest revenue in the set. A diagnosis step that makes the customer feel seen. A guarantee that reads strong in an ad. A number (93%) and a comparison to minoxidil. Deep tier-2/3 reach that Arata, at 38% marketplace and 30% quick commerce, does not yet have.

**Weaknesses.** Price inconsistency on its own cost page. A five-month lock to earn the refund. Minoxidil in the kit, with the shedding and dependency anxiety the brief records in Arata's own customers. ₹138 Cr of marketing against ₹343 Cr of revenue and a net loss. The 93% claim rests on a 2022 internal study.

**Implications for Arata.** Where Traya is strong versus Arata: diagnosis, guarantee, scale, tier-2/3 distribution. Where Arata is strong (hypothesis until win/loss data exists): no doctor, no minoxidil, no supplements, a single 30-day bottle, a study number per SKU, half the per-month outlay on the Intensive Serum (₹571 versus ₹1,400 to ₹1,800). Opportunity: the Traya drop-out. Anyone who abandoned a kit before month five has spent ₹3,000 to ₹7,000, earned no refund, and still has the problem. Threat: Traya moves down-market with a single-product entry SKU, or adds a non-minoxidil serum at ₹600 to ₹900.
Profile 2: Pilgrim
**Depth:** quick scan. **Priority:** 2. The serum price-band leader on Nykaa and Amazon.

head: At a glance
Value
Source
rows: Ingredient-led; "12-ingredient" hair growth story; Korean-beauty framing

blocks.text: **Positioning.** Pilgrim sells the ingredient. The hero serum headline is the actives and their percentages. The brand story is sourcing (Korean, and in other ranges, French and Australian). The audience is young, female-skewed, Nykaa-native, buying by ingredient recognition. Per the brief, it "falls short" on a clinical number and on a story that is generic to the category.
**Pricing.** ₹595 to ₹699 for the 30 ml hero serum, per the brief. Bundles, subscriptions and multi-packs: not observed in this snapshot, to be checked at the first deep profile.

**Strengths.** The largest actives-led brand in the set by revenue. Strong marketplace ratings presence (counts to be pulled from Nykaa and Amazon at re-profile). A wide catalogue that lets a customer buy a full routine in one brand, which the brief lists as something Arata also offers but has not productised with a routine builder.
**Weaknesses.** Same Redensyl + Anagain stack as Minimalist, Bare Anatomy and ThriveCo. Differentiation by ingredient story alone. No study number on the serum as observed.

**Implications.** Pilgrim is the brand Arata's ₹571 Intensive Serum is compared against on a Nykaa results page. Arata is ₹24 to ₹128 cheaper and carries a number (up to 28,200 new hairs in 84 days) where Pilgrim carries a percentage of actives. The ad line writes itself once the price is confirmed on the day the ad runs. Threat: Pilgrim adds a consumer-study number to its serum. It has the revenue to fund one.
Profile 3: Minimalist
**Depth:** quick scan. **Priority:** 3. The concentration-disclosure benchmark.

head: At a glance
Value
Source
rows: Majority acquired by Hindustan Unilever, announced January 2025
Brief; 1mg and PharmEasy listing titles, Oct 2026
Listed as "Hair Growth Actives 18%" on Indian pharmacies and "Hair Density Serum 18%" on an overseas retailer
Not observed on pages checked, as of 10 Oct 2026

blocks.text: **Positioning.** Minimalist sells transparency. The number on the pack is the percentage of actives, and the brand's authority comes from disclosing it. The tone is clinical and plain. The brief calls the brand "cold" and notes that it requires ingredient literacy and offers no routine.

**Inferred (medium confidence).** With Unilever as majority owner, Minimalist now has access to retail distribution and research budgets that the other actives-led brands do not. This is worth watching because Unilever Ventures also sits on Arata's cap table, which may shape how aggressively either side runs direct comparison.
**Strengths.** Trust from disclosure. Fragrance-free appeals to the sensitive-scalp buyer Arata's Dandruff Divya persona resembles. Deep pockets post-acquisition.

**Weaknesses.** No routine. No warmth. The 18% is an input number, and the customer cannot feel 18%. The naming drift across listings (Actives versus Density) mirrors Arata's own onion/biotin and serum/tonic inconsistency, so this is a weakness Arata should fix in itself before pointing at it.

**Implications.** Minimalist is the comparison for Clinical Kavya at the ₹700 tier. Arata's answer is an output number (28,200 new hairs; 7.4X) versus an input number (18%). The cleanest line in the category: "They tell you what is in the bottle. We tell you what it did." Threat: Unilever-funded consumer studies that put an output number on Minimalist's pack within a year.
Profile 4: Bare Anatomy (Innovist)
**Depth:** quick scan. **Priority:** 4. The only rival with a quiz, which is on Arata's known-gaps list.

head: At a glance
Value
Source
rows: Innovist (also owns other D2C personal-care brands)
"Advanced Hair Growth Serum: 3% Redensyl + 4% Anagain + Rosemary + Rice Water"
Not observed on pages checked, as of 10 Oct 2026

blocks.text: **Positioning.** "Made for you" personalisation through a quiz that outputs a routine. The brief's reading is that the personalisation is cosmetic: the actives behind the quiz are the same Redensyl + Anagain stack at the same ₹649 price point.

**Strengths.** The quiz. It converts the customer's anxiety ("which one is for me?") into a cart, which is exactly the job Arata's Routine Ritika persona needs done. It also captures first-party data at the top of the funnel.
**Weaknesses.** Same actives as three other brands. Personalisation that does not change the formula. Smaller than Pilgrim and Minimalist by revenue (per the brief's ordering; figures to be pulled).

**Implications.** Bare Anatomy proves the quiz mechanic works in this category. Arata has no quiz and no routine builder (brief, known gaps). The opportunity is to ship a quiz that routes to a study-backed routine rather than a personalised label. The threat is small on product and real on funnel: a quiz brand will out-convert a catalogue brand on cold traffic until Arata has one.
Profile 5: Mamaearth (Honasa Consumer)
**Depth:** quick scan. **Priority:** 5 for messaging, 1 for quick-commerce shelf watch.

blocks.text: **Positioning.** Mamaearth sells reassurance at scale. The story is ingredient safety and nature, the hero is onion, and the channel is everywhere: general trade, modern trade, every marketplace and every quick-commerce app. Arata's own customers have usually already tried an onion product (brief: "has tried onion shampoo and biotin gummies; nothing showed a number").

**Strengths.** Distribution and recall. Default status on quick commerce. A listed-company balance sheet. The price point a teenager can afford, which Arata's reviews say Arata is not ("on pricier side for a teenager like me").

**Weaknesses.** No proof. A "natural" story the category has moved past, which is the same story Arata itself left behind when it dropped "zero chemicals". Onion as an active has no study number the brief could find.

**Implications.** Mamaearth is the "before" in Arata's customer story. The push in the brief's switching dynamics ("mass shampoo did nothing; onion/biotin products were a gimmick") is a Mamaearth customer talking. For quick commerce, the pitch to a Blinkit category manager is that Arata is the trade-up SKU for the customer Mamaearth has already acquired. Threat: Mamaearth adds a clinically-tested sub-line at ₹399 to ₹499 with a number on the pack, on a shelf it already owns.

Axes: commitment the customer must make (one bottle → multi-month medical programme) against the kind of proof on the pack (none → an outcome number from a study).

**Interpretation.** The top-left quadrant has one brand in it. Four competitors sit in the bottom-left: one bottle, no outcome number. One sits top-right: an outcome number you can only reach through a five-month medical kit. Arata's position is low commitment with a study number, and nobody else occupies it. The whitespace is also the risk: it is empty because it is hard to hold. The number has to survive scrutiny, and the brand has to keep making new numbers (MitoActive's 87% is the first in the new line).

blocks.text: **Inferred (high confidence):** three of the four actives-led brands carry the identical 3% Redensyl + 4% Anagain stack. The category below ₹700 has commoditised on inputs. Arata's Intensive Serum is the only product in that band that claims an output.
Key takeaways

items: MitoActive's real competitor is Traya, and the honest comparison is on commitment and composition. On price, per day the two are within ₹3 of each other at Traya's cheapest tier.

The Intensive Serum at ₹571 is the cheapest hair-growth serum among the actives-led brands and the only one with an outcome number. That is a lead Arata is under-using while the pack-of-3 at ₹999 trains customers to wait for 49% off.

Two competitor mechanics are missing at Arata and sit on its own known-gaps list: a quiz (Bare Anatomy, Traya) and a monthly cadence (Traya). Both are funnel features, and both are buildable without a new formula.
Mamaearth is the brand Arata's customers come from. The right posture is trade-up, and the right venue is the quick-commerce shelf.
Every "not observed" in the comparison table stays a question until it is checked on the competitor's own page. Only then does it become a line Arata can use.

blocks.text: The system

Profiles decay. Pricing pages move within a quarter, claims move with every campaign, and a single snapshot cannot support "they still do not have X". So the deliverable is a loop, with owners and dates, and a folder layout that lets the next run diff against this one.

blocks.text: Priority order and why

items: **Traya, deep profile now.** It defines the MitoActive buyer's alternative and has the most moving parts (three price figures on one page, a conditional guarantee, a kit whose contents vary by stage). Every MitoActive asset depends on this profile being current.
**Pilgrim, quick scan now, deep profile at day 60.** Owns the Nykaa serum comparison. The Arata vs Pilgrim page needs its hero price verified on publish day and again each month.
**Minimalist, quick scan now.** Watch for an outcome study after the Unilever acquisition. Add an alert on any Minimalist press release containing "clinical" or "study".
**Bare Anatomy, quick scan now, funnel walk-through at day 30.** Someone on the Brew team takes the quiz, records every screen, and we build Arata's quiz brief from what works and what does not.
**Mamaearth, shelf watch weekly.** Not a messaging rival. A quick-commerce rival. Track its onion SKUs' placement, price and offer on Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart in Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore.

blocks.text: What the profiles change at Arata
Each recommendation names the profile it comes from, what to do, and the effect we expect.

**From Traya: reframe the MitoActive objection script.** Replace "compare to Traya at ₹1,400 to ₹1,800 a month" with a commitment comparison: one ₹1,499 bottle, no doctor, no minoxidil, no five-month lock, no order-date audit to get a refund. Expected effect: the ₹1,499 objection stops being a price argument Arata loses by ₹3 a day and becomes a composition argument it wins outright. Label: the per-day parity is observed; the win is a hypothesis until the MitoActive page converts against it.

**From Traya: price MitoActive as a course.** Traya's table rewards the six-month commitment with the lowest per-day price. MitoActive's own headline claim is an 84-day claim. A three-bottle 84-day course priced so the per-day figure lands under ₹47 would undercut Traya's cheapest day with a single, non-medical product. The exact price is a pricing-discipline decision; the profile supplies the ceiling.

**From Pilgrim, Minimalist, Bare Anatomy: one line for the ₹571 serum.** The three brands disclose inputs. Arata discloses an output. Every Intensive Serum asset should carry the contrast: what it did, in 84 days, in a study. Expected effect: a reason to choose Arata on the Nykaa results page that does not depend on being ₹24 cheaper.

**From Bare Anatomy and Traya: build the quiz.** Both convert anxiety into a routine before the customer compares serums. Arata's quiz should route by concern (hair fall, dandruff, grey, damage, style) to a named routine with one price and the study number for that routine. Expected effect: higher first-purchase conversion on cold traffic and a first-party data layer for reorder nudges. This closes a gap on the brand's own list.

**From Mamaearth: a trade-up pitch for quick commerce.** The Blinkit and Zepto category pitch says: the onion customer is already in your app and already dissatisfied (brief, verbatim customer language). Arata is the ₹359 to ₹571 step up with a number on the pack. Expected effect: better placement in the hair-fall search results on quick commerce, where 30% of Arata's revenue already comes from.

**From all five: fix the naming drift first.** The profiles caught Minimalist's "Actives" versus "Density" naming across channels. Arata has the same problem (onion versus biotin, serum versus tonic). Before any comparison page points at a rival's inconsistency, Arata's own listings are reconciled. This is a credibility rule, and it costs nothing.

## Landscape in one paragraph
Indian online haircare for hair fall splits into three shapes. A medical
programme (Traya) with a diagnosis, a monthly kit, minoxidil and a
conditional guarantee at ₹1,400 to ₹1,800 a month. An actives-led shelf
(Pilgrim, Minimalist, Bare Anatomy) where three brands sell the same
3% Redensyl + 4% Anagain stack at ₹595 to ₹699 and differ by story:
ingredient origin, disclosed concentration, or a quiz. A mass-natural
default (Mamaearth) that owns distribution and carries no proof. Arata
sits in a fourth position: one bottle, an actives-band price, and an
outcome number from a study on every SKU, with MitoActive at ₹1,499
reaching into the programme band without the programme.

## Key takeaways
1. MitoActive competes with Traya on commitment and composition; per day the prices match.
2. The ₹571 serum is the cheapest and the only one with an outcome number.
3. Quiz and monthly cadence are the two rival mechanics Arata lacks.
4. Mamaearth is the source of Arata's customers, so the posture is trade-up.
5. "Not observed" is a question until checked on the rival's page.

## Gaps and opportunities
- No actives-led brand offers an 84-day course with a per-day price.
- No brand below ₹700 offers a guarantee; Traya's needs five months.
- No brand in the set markets to the Traya drop-out.
- No brand pairs a quiz with a study-backed routine.

Example 3: SWOT, Pilgrim versus Arata

**Strengths (theirs versus ours).** Revenue above ₹200 Cr against Arata's ₹61 Cr. Established Nykaa and Amazon rankings in the hair growth serum results. A wider catalogue across hair, skin and body under one ingredient-story umbrella.

**Weaknesses (theirs versus ours).** The hero serum's headline is 3% Redensyl + 4% Anagain, the same stack Bare Anatomy lists. No outcome number observed on the serum (pages checked 10 Oct 2026). Priced ₹24 to ₹128 above Arata's Intensive Serum.

**Opportunities (for Arata).** The Nykaa results page, where a ₹571 serum with "up to +28,200 new hair in 84 days" sits beside a ₹699 serum with an ingredient list. The customer who has already bought Redensyl once and wants a reason the second bottle will be different. The "Arata vs Pilgrim" page, which should lead with the output-versus-input contrast and show both prices with the date they were checked.

**Threats (from Pilgrim).** A consumer study on the hero serum, which Pilgrim can afford. A price move to ₹549 that erases Arata's price edge, which is why the weekly price watch exists. Deeper quick-commerce placement that takes the default slot Arata is competing with Mamaearth for.

**Decisions this SWOT asks Arata to make.** Publish the Arata vs Pilgrim page in the next 30 days with dated prices. Stop discounting the Intensive Serum below Pilgrim's floor through the pack-of-3, because the price edge is already there at ₹571. Fund the Lab Notes explainer for the 28,200 study design, because the output claim is the entire edge and it has to be legible.
